questions.q: Define therapeutic alliance and state its two major components as per NCERT Class 12 Psychology Chapter 5.
questions.a: Therapeutic alliance is the special confidential interpersonal relationship between client and therapist that serves as the vehicle for change. Its two major components are: (1) the contractual nature — a voluntary partnership between two willing individuals aimed at helping the client overcome problems, and (2) limited duration — the alliance lasts only until the client can deal with problems and take control of their life. A wrong answer that omits "limited duration" or describes it as a permanent friendship reveals confusion between therapeutic alliance and social relationships.

questions.q: A client tells their therapist: "I stole money from my parents last week." The therapist responds: "I understand you're going through a tough time, but stealing is wrong." Identify which core condition of therapeutic alliance is violated and explain why.
questions.a: Unconditional positive regard (UPR) is violated. UPR means the therapist's positive warmth is not contingent on the client's disclosures or behaviours — the therapist accepts the client fully even when the client reveals "wrong" actions. The therapist's moral judgment ("stealing is wrong") makes acceptance conditional. A student who says "empathy is violated" confuses empathy (feeling with the client) with UPR (accepting the client regardless of content).

questions.q: Design a brief "therapy contract" for a 16-year-old client with social anxiety. Include three contractual elements from NCERT and explain how each supports the therapeutic alliance.
questions.a: Contract elements: (1) Voluntary partnership — both client and therapist willingly enter the relationship; supports alliance by establishing agency. (2) Limited duration — therapy ends when client can manage anxiety independently; supports alliance by preventing dependency. (3) Confidentiality — what is shared stays private unless harm risk; supports alliance by enabling trust for self-disclosure. A weak answer lists generic rules (e.g., "be on time") instead of NCERT-specified contractual features.

questions.q: Compare and contrast empathy, sympathy, and intellectual understanding using a single client statement: "I feel like a failure because I didn't get into my dream college."
questions.a: Empathy: "It sounds like you're feeling devastated and questioning your worth right now" — therapist feels WITH the client, adopts client's perspective. Sympathy: "Oh, you poor thing, that's so unfortunate" — therapist feels compassion/pity FOR the client but remains separate. Intellectual understanding: "Statistically, many students don't get their first choice" — cold, factual, no emotional resonance. A student who equates empathy with sympathy misses the critical "feeling like the other person" (perspective-taking) component.

questions.q: Critique this statement: "The therapeutic alliance is just a professional friendship where the therapist is nice to the client so they open up."
questions.a: The statement is inaccurate because: (1) Alliance is contractual and time-limited, not open-ended like friendship. (2) Therapist's warmth is professional (unconditional positive regard), not personal affection. (3) Confidentiality is legally/ethically bound, unlike friendship. (4) Therapist does not reciprocate self-disclosure. (5) Goal is client's autonomous functioning, not mutual enjoyment. A student who agrees confuses the "trusting and confiding" property with informal social support.

questions.q: Create a 3-minute role-play script between a therapist and a client that demonstrates ALL three components of therapeutic alliance (contractual nature, empathy, UPR) in the first session. Annotate each line with the component it illustrates.
questions.a:
Sample script:
Therapist: "Welcome. Our work together is a voluntary partnership — we'll meet weekly for about 12 sessions, and everything you share stays confidential unless safety is at risk." [Contractual: voluntary, limited duration, confidentiality]
Client: "I've been having panic attacks before exams. I feel like I'm losing my mind."
Therapist: "It sounds terrifying to feel your body spiral out of control when you most need to focus." [Empathy: reflects feeling + perspective]
Client: "I skipped my last two exams. I'm such a coward."
Therapist: "You're being very hard on yourself. I want you to know that whatever you share here — even things you're ashamed of — doesn't change my respect for you or my commitment to our work." [UPR: explicit non-contingent acceptance]
A poor script misses one component or shows the therapist giving advice instead of demonstrating the conditions.
